title: Why sharing rovers cuts the wait
summary: Letting every rover take any company's job cuts the mean wait of urgent cargo by {{r:market_cut}}, with the same rovers.
notes: E1 main table and paired differences (results/table_main.csv, table_paired_E1.csv), E19 fleet x job rule x autonomy (results/table_E19.csv). Step scenes are gallery packages (data/scenes/gallery.json). Wording for LEAD to edit.

steps.title: Two ways to run the rovers
steps.text: Each company can keep its own rovers for its own cargo. Or every rover can take any job, offered in a small auction to whichever rover can finish it soonest.
steps.visual: The base from above; each rover is coloured by the company that owns it.

steps.title: Own rovers, own queue
steps.text: With in-house fleets an urgent item waits {{r:inhouse_mean}} on average in the second phase of the base, and one in ten waits more than {{r:inhouse_p90}}. Only {{r:inhouse_sl24}} arrive within a day.
steps.visual: Cargo piles up at a pad while a rover of another company stands idle nearby.

steps.title: Any rover, any job
steps.text: When every rover can take any job, the mean wait falls to {{r:market_mean}} and the slow tail to {{r:market_p90}}: {{r:market_cut}} less waiting with the same rovers. {{r:market_sl24}} of urgent items now arrive within a day.
steps.visual: The same moment with the shared job rule: the idle rover picks up the waiting cargo.

steps.title: The auction beats first come, first served
steps.text: Sharing alone does most of the work, but the auction adds to it: {{r:vs_greedy}} less waiting than handing each job to the nearest free rover, in paired runs.
steps.visual: Bids from several rovers appear over a new job; the earliest finisher wins it.

steps.title: It matters most when rovers are few
steps.text: With {{r:e19_rovers}}, sharing cuts the urgent wait from {{r:e19_inhouse}} to {{r:e19_market}}. Autonomous driving brings it down to {{r:e19_auto}}.
steps.visual: A small fleet crossing the base, every rover busy.
